source.title: Engineering Monosemanticity in Toy Models
source.authors: A. Jermyn; Nicholas Schiefer; Evan Hubinger

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures monosemanticity in trained toy networks and tests how it changes with training choices, capacity, and task conditions; it does not reproduce the original vision-neuron analyses.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for toy networks on feature-decoder, random re-projector, and absolute-value tasks. Discussion of results from cited work is not recorded as study results. SoLU experiments are mentioned, but the authors say they stopped without clear results. Individual training traces and figure points are not transcribed when the text gives only aggregate descriptions.
record.test_reason: In controlled toy networks the study measures how often neurons are polysemantic (activation-ratio measure). It varies width (capacity), feature density, learning rate, bias initialization, weight decay, L1 regularization and activation function, and reports loss alongside. This bears directly on V3, V4 and V5. It never examines vision or language models.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, with three additions. The authors find that with feature-sparse inputs, models can be made more monosemantic at no loss cost by changing which minimum training reaches. Moderate negative bias marks the more monosemantic minima and can be used to engineer them. Wider layers give more monosemantic neurons, at compute cost, and naive weight sparsity degraded performance. They (weakly) view polysemanticity as how the model copes with too few neurons. A residual ~d polysemantic neurons implement a low-rank identity. They call the bias-decay method fragile and still do not understand the most polysemantic models' algorithm.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses controlled toy feature tasks and a single-neuron activation-ratio measure, rather than analysis of naturally occurring vision-model neurons or feature visualization.
record.method_sensitivity: Monosemanticity varies with learning rate, initial bias, bias weight-decay schedule, task, feature frequency, nonlinear-layer width, activation function, and L1 regularization.
record.problems: The evidence concerns toy tasks rather than vision or language models. The authors describe some conclusions as preliminary or weakly held, report no uncertainty estimates in the text, and say they lack clear results for SoLU. Their monosemanticity threshold is acknowledged to be arbitrary.
record.rows_left_out: Individual plotted training traces, figure points, and intermediate conditions are not listed separately where the paper gives only aggregate trend descriptions; see Figures 1, 3, 6–9, 12, 15–23. SoLU is omitted because the authors report no clear result.

untested.parts: Not tested: vision classifiers and InceptionV1 neurons.
Not tested: transformer language-model MLP neurons and layer dependence.
Not tested: whether superposition causes polysemanticity in real trained networks.
Not tested: initialization noise as a separate cause (only the mean bias offset is varied); real models.
Not tested: SoLU (attempted, but no clear results), modern convnets, real models.
Not tested: the whole version; no canonical neurons are reassessed.
Not tested: alternative activation ranges or scoring methods. The threshold of 0.999 is fixed, though Figure 2 shows the cumulative distribution.

missing.what: Dependence of monosemanticity on initial mean bias and feature density. For bias below about −√ε, 30–50% of neurons are monosemantic, with a sharp drop above that.
With negative bias, a large fraction of neurons become monosemantic even when k<N, at no loss cost. The monosemantic fraction peaks at one neuron per feature.
Power-law feature-frequency replications of the learning-rate, bias and width results.
Preliminary result: a regularizer pulling biases toward negative values yields more monosemantic models than zero-bias initialization.

record.verdict_notes: These are toy networks with a known feature basis, and polysemanticity is measured by a single-feature activation-ratio threshold (r_i>0.999). No uncertainty estimates are reported. The paper is not an original source for any version. The record's V5 limits_scope verdict citing R11 was wrong, since more monosemantic models had lower loss; R11 now counts toward V5 support. The polysemantic neurons here often fire for most features, not for a few unrelated ones.

versions.untested_parts: Image classifiers, InceptionV1, and the example of a vision neuron responding to cat faces and cars.
Transformer language models, MLP neurons, and token or context responses.
The paper studies toy networks and capacity-related conditions, not whether superposition is the general cause of polysemanticity in trained networks.
The paper tests toy networks and training path dependence; it does not isolate initialization, regularization, and training noise as separate general causes across architectures.
Modern convnets are not tested. SoLU was tried but the authors report no clear results.
The study does not reassess canonical neurons in real models or test whether their apparently unrelated inputs share a feature.
The study defines a monosemanticity measure and chooses a threshold, but does not compare alternative activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

rows.subject: feature decoder toy model
rows.size_stated: N=512 features, d=64 input dimensions, k=1024 neurons
rows.operation_detail: Trained with different learning rates from zero-mean initial bias.
rows.measure: Task loss and number of monosemantic neurons
rows.baseline: Different learning-rate runs compared with one another; no separate numerical baseline stated.
rows.value: The final models have indistinguishable loss but very different numbers of monosemantic neurons; higher learning rates find more monosemantic solutions.
rows.note: The authors describe runs with k greater than the number of features and say the loss is indistinguishable across the different monosemanticity basins.
rows.check: k=1024 exceeds N=512, yet low-LR runs are mostly polysemantic at equal loss. This shows polysemanticity without capacity pressure (V4, V5 observed). For V3 it qualifies capacity as the sole cause.

rows.subject: feature decoder toy model
rows.size_stated: N=512 features, d=64 input dimensions, k=1024 neurons
rows.operation_detail: Initialized biases with a negative mean and used bias weight decay during training.
rows.baseline: Models trained without the negative-initial-bias intervention
rows.value: The intervention produces highly monosemantic solutions across the tested learning rates, with loss comparable to models trained without it.
rows.note: Weight decay was turned off for the final 50% of training so the final models were minima without weight decay.

rows.subject: feature decoder toy model
rows.size_stated: N=512 features, d=64 input dimensions, k=1024 neurons
rows.operation_detail: Measured each neuron's responses to single-feature inputs in the highest-learning-rate model.

rows.subject: feature decoder toy model
rows.size_stated: N=512 features, d=64 input dimensions; k varied from 16 to 2048
rows.measure: Task loss and number of monosemantic neurons
rows.value: More neurons produce more monosemantic neurons. Loss decreases as width grows until the number of neurons exceeds the number of features; beyond that, loss gains diminish while additional neurons mostly increase the monosemantic-neuron count.
rows.note: The authors report the sweep as a trend across model widths rather than as a single aggregate numerical estimate.

rows.subject: feature decoder toy model
rows.operation_detail: Compared zero and negative initial mean biases across layer widths.
rows.value: For widths 16–128, loss plateaus were indistinguishable; for widths 256, 384, and 512, negative-bias models performed slightly worse; above 512 neurons, negative-bias models outperformed zero-bias models.
rows.note: This result qualifies the claim that more monosemantic models can be obtained without a performance cost: the loss difference depends on width.
rows.check: State changed from partial. The authors say the negative bias 'usually does not come at any significant performance cost'. They describe only 'slightly worse' loss at widths 256–512, which is consistent with V5's 'without a large loss'. The width-dependent sign of the loss difference fits V3's capacity reading, which the authors call weakly held.

conditions.value: varied up to the regime where Nε exceeds d

rows.value: Monosemanticity peaks around ε=2^-5 ≈ 0.03; it declines as feature frequency rises, and by Nε ≈ 2d there are almost no monosemantic neurons left.
rows.note: The authors describe a smooth transition around the regime where the expected number of active features approaches the embedding dimension, not a sharp phase transition.
rows.check: Feature frequency is a property of the data, not of architecture or training, so the V5 link is removed.

rows.subject: random re-projector toy model
rows.size_stated: N=512 features, d=64 input dimensions; k=1024 neurons
rows.operation_detail: Trained with a negative initial mean bias across learning rates.
rows.value: The models reached roughly one monosemantic neuron per feature across a range of learning rates.

rows.subject: absolute value toy model
rows.size_stated: N=512 features, d=64 input dimensions, k=2048 neurons
rows.operation_detail: Trained models with different learning rates and compared their monosemanticity and loss.
rows.measure: Task loss and number of monosemantic neurons
rows.value: Unlike the decoder and re-projector models, models with different monosemanticity achieve different losses; more monosemantic models have lower loss.
rows.note: This qualifies the claim that monosemanticity can be increased without a performance cost.
rows.check: More monosemantic solutions have lower loss, so this is not a performance cost of reducing polysemanticity. The record's note treating it as a cost is wrong. With k=2048>N, polysemantic basins still arise (V4). For V3 this qualifies capacity as the sole cause.

rows.subject: absolute value toy model
rows.size_stated: N=512 features, d=64 input dimensions, k=2048 neurons
rows.operation_detail: Varied weight decay rate for models initialized with negative bias.
rows.baseline: Models with different weight decay rates
rows.value: A negative initial bias alone did not reliably produce mostly monosemantic models; slower weight decay produced more monosemantic solutions, and the authors report that combining negative initial bias with slow weight decay appeared sufficient for highly monosemantic models.
rows.note: The authors hypothesize that slow decay gives the more complicated task time to learn while biases remain in a useful range.
rows.check: Polysemantic outcomes depend on the weight-decay rate, i.e. on regularization, which is what V4 names. State changed from partial to observed for V4. For V5 it shows that the negative-bias method alone is insufficient on this task.

rows.subject: feature decoder toy model
rows.size_stated: N=512 features, d=64 input dimensions; width varied
rows.operation_detail: Applied fixed Erdős–Rényi sparsity to the linear layers and compared performance at fixed compute cost.
rows.baseline: Dense layers at fixed compute cost
rows.value: Even modest sparsity resulted in significantly greater loss; dense layers were more performant at fixed compute cost.
rows.note: This tests the proposed way of reducing the computational cost of wider layers; the text does not give a numerical loss difference.
rows.check: Monosemanticity is not measured. The row reports only the loss of sparse versus dense layers at fixed compute. It bears on the compute cost of the width route, not on the polysemantic share.

tranche.reason: It uses a different toy architecture and an activation-ratio measure to ask the same question: when are neurons polysemantic?

source_check.notes: Preliminary toy-model work; the authors call some views weakly held. Appendix A says code is on GitHub, so the record header's code n is wrong. Table 1 columns are garbled, so the absolute-value width k=2048 is inferred. The weight decay in the negative-bias scheme acts on biases only. SoLU was tried with no clear results. The ~d residual count is a bias proxy, confirmed by activations only at d=64.

statements.correction: Negative- vs zero-bias loss: indistinguishable at k=16-128, slightly worse at k=256/384/512 (k<=N), better at k>512 (Sec 4.1.4). Monosemanticity peaks at ε=2^-5 (Nε=d/4), then falls smoothly; almost no monosemantic neurons by Nε≈2d (Sec 4.1.5).
statements.problem: Says monosemantic models do worse only when k<N. The text shows slightly worse loss at k=256, 384 and 512, and 512 equals N. The 'approaches 2d' phrasing is loose: the rise starts at Nε=d/4.

statements.correction: Transition begins at ε=2^-5 (Nε=d/4). The Nε=d line lies near the transition (Fig 18). Almost no monosemantic neurons by Nε≈2d. The change is smooth, with no sharp phase transition. The comparison is with embedding dimension d (64), not neuron count k (1024).
statements.problem: Places the threshold at Nε approaching 2d. The text puts the change around Nε≈d: it starts at d/4 and is near-complete by 2d. No threshold at 2d is stated.

statements.correction: Code: the text states the model and training code are available on GitHub (Appendix A; URL lost in extraction).
statements.problem: The 'why' line gives code n, but the text says an implementation is available on GitHub. The findings themselves are right.

statements.correction: Code is available on GitHub per Appendix A. 65 positive-bias neurons at d=64 (k=1024, LR3); 33 at d=32 and 130 at d=128 with bias >0.05 as the proxy. k is not stated for the d=32 and d=128 runs.
statements.problem: The 'why' line gives code n, but the text says the code is on GitHub. Counts and proxy are right.

statements.correction: 2211.09169: widths k=16-2048 for N=512 (Fig 15-17, R4). Above k=N, extra neurons mostly add monosemantic neurons. No polysemantic-neuron count against width is reported. The absolute-value runs use k=2048 (Table 1, garbled).
statements.problem: Calls 2312.03096 'the one study that varies width'. 2211.09169 also sweeps width, from k=16 to 2048 with N=512, including k=1024 and 2048 > N. Its tested capacity goes up to k=2048, not only 1024.

statements.correction: 2211.09169, absolute-value task (k=2048>N, initial bias -1): slower bias weight decay gives more monosemantic models (Fig 23, R12). Sec 4.1.3: too high a decay rate gives more polysemantic solutions. The decay acts only on biases, inside the negative-bias scheme.
statements.problem: Says only the l1 experiment shows regularization producing polysemanticity and that weight decay goes the other way. In 2211.09169, faster (bias) weight decay gives more polysemantic models at k>N. The study's own R12 verdict reads this as regularization.

statements.correction: Code is available on GitHub per Appendix A. GeLU decoder (batch B3): monosemanticity is sharply peaked near initial bias -1, just below the GeLU minimum, and the peak shifts slightly with learning rate.
statements.problem: The 'why' line says no code for 2211.09169, but the text says the code is on GitHub. The GeLU result is right.

statements.correction: Feature decoder: the negative-bias model has loss comparable to the best L1 model in the body text (lower in the Fig 14 caption), with comparable monosemanticity. Absolute value: more monosemantic solutions have lower loss. Code is on GitHub.
statements.problem: Puts the L1 comparison in the absolute-value task, but it is a feature-decoder result (Sec 4.1.3). The body says comparable loss and only the Fig 14 caption says lower. The 'why' line also says no code, but the text says it is on GitHub.

statements.correction: Absolute value, bias -1: a negative bias alone does not robustly give mostly monosemantic models. Monosemanticity rises with learning rate (Fig 22), and slower bias decay also gives more monosemantic models (Fig 23). Decoder: slightly worse loss at k=256-512.
statements.problem: Says a negative bias alone fails without slow weight decay. The text says either a high learning rate or a low weight-decay rate is needed, so slow decay is not the only fix.

statements.correction: Absolute value, bias -1: a high learning rate or a low bias weight-decay rate is needed for mostly monosemantic models (Sec 4, Fig 22-23).
statements.problem: Says a negative bias alone fails without slow weight decay. The text also names a high learning rate as an alternative.
